report:
**Conclusion:** The evidence does **not** support the claim that giving more childhood vaccines causes more autism.

The concern is understandable because autism signs are often recognized during the same years that children receive many vaccines; timing alone, however, cannot show causation. The original prominent MMR-autism report was a small case series, not a study capable of establishing cause and effect, and it was later retracted. [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3136032/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3136032/)

Most directly relevant to “more vaccines” is a U.S. case-control study that totaled the immune-stimulating antigens children received from vaccines in the first two years. Children with autism had no greater antigen exposure than controls; risk did not rise with antigen exposure. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/)

A 2014 meta-analysis combining cohort and case-control evidence likewise found no association between autism and vaccination, MMR, thimerosal/mercury, or vaccine exposure assessed across the included studies. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24814559/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24814559/)

This is also consistent with a very large Danish nationwide cohort study of more than 650,000 children: MMR vaccination was not associated with autism, including among groups considered at higher baseline risk. Its result does not alone test every possible vaccine schedule, but it is strong evidence against the best-known proposed vaccine link. [https://autismsciencefoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/vaccine.2019.pdf](https://autismsciencefoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/vaccine.2019.pdf)

No medical intervention is risk-free, and vaccine safety monitoring remains important. But the specific “increasing number of childhood vaccines increases autism” claim has been tested in large observational studies and evidence syntheses and has not been borne out.
